newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS-Watchdog suspends Spanish utility shares.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Watchdog suspends Spanish utility shares.

text.p: Spain's bourse watchdog CNMV suspended trading in the shares of Hidrocantabrico and four other electrical groups on Monday, reflecting a shake-up in the once cosy sector in the final weeks before liberalisation.

It suspended trade in Hidrocantabrico, Electra de Viesgo and Saltos del Nansa following a report in a daily newspaper that Hidrocantabrico was studying the purchase of a controlling stake in the two groups.

The Gaceta de los Negocios said Hidrocantabrico was looking at buying 91 percent of Viesgo and a controlling stake in Saltos del Nansa, both of which are now in the hands of the market leader, 66-percent state-owned Endesa.
Such purchases would convert Hidrocantabrico into the fourth largest electrical group in Spain after Endesa, Iberdrola and Union Fenosa, the report said.

It followed the government's approval of a plan under which Endesa would purchase up to 75 percent of regional electrical distributors in Andalucia and Catalunya in order to secure its position before full privatisation by 1999.
Shares in the the two distributors, Electricidad de Sevillana and Fuerzas Electricas de Catalunya (Fecsa), were also suspended on Monday in the wake of the report.

Under the plan, Endesa must divest holdings it currently has in other groups such as in Viesgo, Union Fenosa and Nansa, the report said. But for its part, Endesa said it had no plans to sell Viesgo or Nansa.

The tumult in the the electrical sector, the backbone of Spain's stock market, stems largely from the upcoming liberalisation of the long-protected sector, with an end to generous rate increases that ensured comfortable profit margins.

On Friday, Industry Minister Josep Pique said Spain would prepare a new framework for the electricity sector in coming weeks, which would introduce complete competition in both the generation and distribution of energy.
Analysts welcomed the report of possible deals, saying the various purchases would ensure competition and level out differences, preparing the groups for the new sector framework.

"The (new) groups will be levelled out in terms of their distribution and generating set-up and mix and the changes should be beneficial to the sector," said one utilities analyst at a Spanish brokerage.
Despite Endesa's denial, analysts said they expected the sales to go through and argued that they would be beneficial to Hidrocantabrico.

"Previously Cantabrico was merely a generator and highly dependent on coal. It it is confirmed (that it is to buy Viesgo and Nansa), it will benefit, because not only will it gain distribution quota but also it will have hydro potential. Its generating mix will improve," one analyst said.

Should the deals go ahead, giants Endesa and Iberdrola would take up 80 percent of the market, the Fenosa group would account for around 15 percent and the Cantabrico group would take up the rest, analysts said.
